title: Routines in one picture: charters and people

story: Imagine a Tuesday morning without this lesson. A pull request appears on fcp from rhino-ai-agents[bot], the GitHub App every agent uses: "Fix flaky upload test". It changes eleven files in cloud/ and lowers a coverage threshold in pyproject.toml. Nobody on the team asked for it. In Slack, three people ask the same three questions: which bot is this, what was it allowed to touch, and who should review it? The only answers are inside a prompt that nobody reviewed.

Nova never has this problem, because a person assigns every ticket to Nova, and that person is the requester. A routine starts by itself, from a red build, a bug ticket or a timer. So before we build a single routine, we need one place where its rules and its people are written down, where anyone can read them, and where code, not the model, makes the rules hold.
hook.question: Where does a routine's rulebook live, and how do we make sure the rules hold and a person answers for every routine?

p: A routine is the same agent as Nova, our ticket-to-PR agent, started by an event instead of an assignment. The events are a red build on main, a dependency PR from Renovate that fails CI, a Bug ticket that a team has triaged, and a timer for the weekly cleanup jobs. Everything after the start is shared with Nova: the same harness (our program in the VM that runs the Claude session), the same fresh VM for every run, the same walls and the same review layers. That is the whole design decision of this part of the course. If routines had their own code, we would build and check the safety walls once for Nova and again for every routine, and one of the copies would drift.

So only two things differ, the trigger and the charter. A charter is one short YAML file per routine in the ai-agents repo, under routines/charters/. Three things are involved every time a routine runs: the trigger that starts it, routineRun (the Temporal workflow that every routine runs), and the charter, which routineRun loads first. The charter answers the questions from the story, in a file that is reviewed in a pull request like any code: who owns the routine, what wakes it, where it may write, and what must be true before it may say it is done. Here is the first one, for the frontend CI fixer.

code.text:
name: fe-ci-fixer
team: fe
stage: shadow                        # shadow, then drafts, then normal
trigger:
  kind: github.workflow_run
  repo: RhinoHealth/fcp
  workflows: ["[FRONTEND] - CI"]
  branch: main
  conclusion: failure
gather_minutes: 7
queue: cifix                         # task queue ai-agents-cifix, 2 VM slots
vm: { size: lite, spot: true }
model: { name: claude-opus-5-5, effort: low, on_failed_checks: medium }
allowed_paths: ["frontend/**"]
denied_paths: [".github/**", "frontend/biome.json", "frontend/tsconfig.json", "frontend/playwright.config.ts"]
never: [edit_test_assertions]
skills: [fix-ci, fe-codebase, verify, fcp-lab, pr-story]
done:
  - the failed job's commands fail on the red commit and pass on the fix, in the VM
  - npm run verify is green
  - no test weakened
pr:
  labels: ["routine:fe-ci-fixer"]

notes.text: Every routine starts in shadow: it runs on real triggers and opens nothing. The trust-ladder lesson moves it up.
What wakes it: frontend CI finishing with a failure on main.
Wait 7 minutes so that every red build with the same cause joins one run. The next lesson builds this.
A small VM on Spot: spare AWS capacity that is cheaper, but that AWS may take back. Fine for a routine nobody is waiting on.
Opus 5.5 at low effort; a step whose checks failed runs again at medium.
Where it may write. The next sections show who enforces this.
Extra rules for this routine: a CI fixer may not change an existing test assertion.
The skills the session loads, at most 6, because more skills crowd the context.
The list the harness checks before the agent may say it is finished.

p: A YAML file can be wrong in a way that nobody notices. Picture one missing letter: denied_path instead of denied_paths. A normal parser reads the file happily, the code looks for denied_paths, finds nothing, and uses an empty list. The wall around .github/ is gone, and there is not a single error anywhere. This is why the charter's schema uses zod's strictObject: any key that the schema does not know is an error, so the typo fails loudly instead of quietly removing a rule.

The same rule refuses keys that nobody implemented. If someone writes max_turns: 50 "to be safe", the load fails, because the platform never cuts an agent short with a turn, time or budget limit, so there is no code behind that key. A test in the ai-agents repo loads every charter in CI, so a broken charter turns its own pull request red, long before a run ever reads it.

notes.text: strictObject: an unknown key is an error, not something to ignore.
Each kind of trigger has its own fields, so the trigger is loose: only kind is checked here.
An empty list would mean "may write nowhere", which is always a mistake, so it is refused.
The three extra rules that the false-heal check knows. A later lesson builds that check.
At least one skill and at most six.
The TypeScript type comes from the schema, so there is only one definition.

deeper.h: Go deeper: why the charter is read at one commit
p: routineRun does not read the charter file directly. Workflow code must be deterministic, because Temporal replays it after a restart, and reading a file is input from outside. So the workflow calls an activity, loadCharter(name, sha), which reads the charter at one commit of the ai-agents repo. A replay then sees exactly the same charter, and a run that started before someone merged a charter change keeps the rules it started with.

read.h: Paths are a wall, not a request
p: Writing "only edit files under frontend/" in a prompt asks the model nicely, and a model that is confused, or that read a poisoned comment, can ignore a polite request. The charter's paths are enforced twice instead, by code. Inside the VM, a PreToolUse hook (the Agent SDK hook that runs before every tool call, from the hooks lesson) refuses every Edit and Write outside allowed_paths, with a short reason the agent can read. The agent sees the refusal and works on something else, and the pull request lists what was refused.

The hook has a blind spot: Bash can change files too, for example with sed -i, and a Bash call has no file path for the hook to check. So the broker's git proxy, which every push goes through, checks every changed path against the same charter at git push. That second check is the real wall. The hook only gives the early, readable refusal. Both use the same small function, so they can never disagree.

notes.text: matchesGlob is in Node's own path module: frontend/** matches every file under frontend/.
Inside an allowed glob and not inside a denied one. The git proxy calls the same function at push.

p: Nova's requester is whoever assigned the ticket. Nobody assigns a red build, so each routine gets an owner: a named person who answers for it, listed in config/people.yaml, the file that already maps each person's Slack, Jira and GitHub names. Every pull request of the routine ends with Requested-by: @<owner>. You know what that line does from the independent-approval lesson: the requester's approval never counts. So the owner is responsible for the routine, and someone else approves its pull requests.

That someone is the reviewer of the day. Each team lists a rotation of GitHub handles. When a routine's pull request is marked ready, the orchestrator picks rotation[workingDayIndex % rotation.length], skips the owner if the rotation lands on them, and requests that one person. There is no CODEOWNERS file and no review request to a whole team, so nobody gets ten pings for one small pull request. A holiday swap is a one-line pull request to people.yaml.

code.text:
teams:
  fe:
    channel: "#fe-guild"
    reviewers: ["gh-maya", "gh-omer", "gh-dana"]   # one per working day, Sunday to Thursday
  be:
    channel: "#be-guild"
    reviewers: ["gh-lior", "gh-noa", "gh-amit", "gh-yael"]
owners:
  fe-ci-fixer: "gh-maya"      # written as Requested-by: on every fe-ci-fixer PR
  be-ci-fixer: "gh-amit"

notes.text: Where the team's daily digest about its routines goes.
The rotation, in order. Working day 0 is Sunday.
The owner answers for the routine and can never be its approver.

lab.title: A charter that refuses mistakes
needs: Node 22.18 or newer (it runs .ts files directly)
lab.goal: Write a routine's charter, load it with a strict schema, and prove with tests that typos, unknown keys and too many skills are refused instead of ignored.

guess.q: A teammate adds max_turns: 50 to the fe-ci-fixer charter "to be safe". The schema uses z.strictObject. What happens when the charter is loaded?

options.why: Nothing in the platform reads such a key, and the platform never limits an agent's turns, so there is nothing that could stop the run.

options.text: The key is ignored and the charter loads.
options.why: That is what z.object does. It is exactly the behaviour we avoid, because the same silence would hide a typo in a real key.
strictObject refuses every key it does not know, so the mistake turns the charter's own pull request red.

follow.say: Make a folder of your own and install the two packages the platform uses for charters: yaml to read the file and zod to check it.

npm init -y >/dev/null && npm pkg set type=module
npm install zod@4 yaml@2 && npm ls

follow.say: Write the schema and the loader in one file, because the loader is only a few lines on top of the schema.
Write a small check that loads every charter and prints what each routine may touch, then run it.
follow.see: ✔ fe-ci-fixer: shadow, queue cifix, edits frontend/**, denied .github/** frontend/biome.json frontend/tsconfig.json

follow.say: Add a key nobody implemented, to see the strict schema refuse it. Then remove it again.
follow.do:
echo "max_turns: 50" >> charters/fe-ci-fixer.yaml && node check.ts
sed -i.bak '/max_turns/d' charters/fe-ci-fixer.yaml

follow.say: Now make the dangerous typo, and then see what a normal, non-strict schema would do with it. This is the reason for strictObject.
follow.do:
sed -i.bak 's/^denied_paths:/denied_path:/' charters/fe-ci-fixer.yaml && node check.ts
sed -i.bak 's/z.strictObject({$/z.object({/' charter.ts && node check.ts

✖ Unrecognized key: "denied_path"
✔ fe-ci-fixer: shadow, queue cifix, edits frontend/**, denied (nothing)

follow.say: Put both files back: strictObject in the schema and the right key in the charter. Then check that the wall is back.
follow.do:
sed -i.bak 's/z.object({$/z.strictObject({/' charter.ts
sed -i.bak 's/^denied_path:/denied_paths:/' charters/fe-ci-fixer.yaml && node check.ts
follow.see: ✔ fe-ci-fixer: shadow, queue cifix, edits frontend/**, denied .github/** frontend/biome.json frontend/tsconfig.json

lab.build: Write a second charter, charters/be-ci-fixer.yaml, for the backend CI fixer: team be, triggered when [CLOUD] - CI or [CLIENT] - CI fails on main, queue cifix, allowed paths cloud/**, client/** and sdk/**, with **/migrations/** denied, and the skills fix-ci, be-codebase, verify, fcp-lab and pr-story. Then write test/charters.test.ts with five tests: every charter in charters/ loads, an unknown key is refused, the denied_path typo is refused, seven skills are refused, and a file whose name does not match its name: key is refused. Build each bad charter in the test by changing the text of fe-ci-fixer.yaml with .replace(), so the charter on disk stays good. Run node --test --test-reporter=spec.
checks: node check.ts prints two lines, one for be-ci-fixer and one for fe-ci-fixer, and be-ci-fixer is denied **/migrations/**.
node --test --test-reporter=spec ends with pass 5 and fail 0.
If you change z.strictObject back to z.object, the typo test and the unknown-key test fail, and the other three still pass.
node allowed.ts frontend/tsconfig.json prints deny, even though it is under frontend/.
You can point to the line in charter.ts that refuses seven skills.
lab.fix: A teammate was annoyed that every new charter key broke CI, so they changed z.strictObject to z.object in charter.ts "to make the schema friendlier". A week later the fe-ci-fixer charter got a careless edit, denied_path: instead of denied_paths:, and the CI fixer changed frontend/tsconfig.json to make a type error disappear. Make the same two changes in your folder, run node check.ts and your tests, and find which test would have caught it. Then repair charter.ts, and explain why "friendlier" was the wrong goal for this file.
explain: Why do routines share Nova's harness, VMs and review layers instead of having their own, simpler code?
A charter has a typo in a key name. What does z.object do with it, what does z.strictObject do, and why does the difference matter for denied_paths?
The hook refuses Edit and Write outside the allowed paths. Why do we still need the check in the broker's git proxy?
lab.done: Two charters load, five tests pass, and you have seen a one-letter typo remove a wall under z.object and fail loudly under z.strictObject.

check.q: What is different between a routine and Nova?

options.text: A routine uses a lighter harness without hooks, because it only fixes small things
options.why: Routines share Nova's harness on purpose. A second harness would mean building and checking every wall twice.

options.text: Only what starts it and its charter; the harness, VMs, walls and review layers are the same
options.why: That is the design: safety is built once, and every routine inherits it.

options.text: A routine may approve its own pull requests once it reaches the normal stage
options.why: No agent ever approves or merges, at any stage. Normal only means clean pull requests are marked ready for a person.

check.q: A charter says denied_path: [".github/**"], with one letter missing. The schema uses z.strictObject. What happens?

options.text: The charter loads and .github/ is denied, because the parser understands what was meant
options.why: Parsers do not guess. The key denied_paths is simply missing.

options.text: The charter loads with nothing denied, so the routine may edit .github/
options.why: That is what a non-strict z.object would do: drop the unknown key and use the empty default. It is the silent failure strictObject exists to prevent.

options.text: Loading fails with Unrecognized key, and the charter's pull request turns red in CI
options.why: strictObject refuses unknown keys, and a test loads every charter in CI, so the typo never reaches a run.

check.q: The owner of fe-ci-fixer approves one of its pull requests, and nobody else does. What happens?

options.text: The independent-approval check fails, because the owner is on the Requested-by: line
options.why: Every routine PR names its owner as the requester, and the requester's approval never counts. The reviewer of the day, or another person, must approve.

options.text: The pull request can merge, because the owner knows the routine best
options.why: Knowing the routine is exactly why the owner answers for it, but approval must come from someone who did not ask for the change.

options.text: The routine is paused for breaking a rule
options.why: Nothing is paused. The required check simply stays red until someone else approves.

p: Charters live in RhinoHealth/ai-agents as routines/charters/<name>.yaml, one per routine. The Charter schema is in shared/src/schemas.ts (z.strictObject, with the type from z.infer), so the orchestrator, the harness and CI read charters the same way. orchestrator/src/routines/charter.ts parses them with the yaml package, and orchestrator/test/charters.test.ts loads every charter in CI. routineRun loads its charter through the loadCharter(name, sha) activity, pinned to an ai-agents commit. The harness passes allowed_paths, denied_paths and never to the session, where the blockProtectedPaths PreToolUse hook is extended with the charter's paths, and the broker's git proxy re-checks every changed path at push.

Default paths per team: FE gets frontend/**; BE gets cloud/**, client/** and sdk/**, with **/migrations/** denied in the pilot; DevOps gets the infrastructure and gitops repos plus .github/**. Lint, type and test config stay denied as locked checks. Optional keys repo, read_only and setup serve routines outside fcp, such as kb-ingest. Each guild fills its teams and owners block in config/people.yaml, and the guilds agree how a Bug counts as triaged into a team (the proposal is the label FE or BE on a Bug in To Do). Before any of this, the old n8n Jira-to-PR story RH-7207 is closed: its useful notes go into the Jira poller ticket, the n8n flow is deactivated (not deleted), and n8n stays for business flows such as Vanil.

tickets.why: Close RH-7207, the n8n Jira-to-PR flow, so agent PRs come from one platform only.
The charter format, the strict schema, the loader pinned to a commit, and the path wall in the hook and the git proxy.
Owners per routine, Requested-by: on every PR, and the reviewer of the day from people.yaml.

words.plain: Nova started by an event, such as a red build, a bug ticket or a timer, instead of by a person assigning a ticket.
One reviewed YAML file per routine: owner, trigger, where it may write, extra rules, skills, model, VM and what done means.
A zod object schema that refuses any key it does not know, so typos fail instead of being ignored.
The person who answers for a routine. Written as Requested-by: on its PRs, so never its approver.
One person from a team's rotation, never the owner, asked to review a routine PR when it is marked ready.

review.q: Name four things a charter says about a routine, and say which of them are enforced by code outside the model.
review.a: For example owner, trigger, allowed and denied paths, never-list, skills, model, VM size and done. Paths are enforced by the PreToolUse hook and again by the broker's git proxy at push; the never-list by the false-heal check; done by the harness before the agent may finish.

review.q: A teammate wants to switch the Charter schema to z.object so new keys stop breaking CI. What do you answer?
review.a: Breaking CI on an unknown key is the point: with z.object a typo like denied_path is dropped silently and a wall disappears. New keys should be added to the schema in the same pull request.

review.q: Why does a routine need a named owner, and why can that owner never approve its pull requests?
review.a: Nobody assigns a red build, so someone must answer for the routine. The owner is written as the requester (Requested-by:), and the independent-approval check never counts the requester's approval, so a second person always looks.

remember: A routine is Nova with a different trigger: its rules live in a strict, reviewed charter that code enforces, and its owner answers for it but never approves it.
